Optimal dose finding with the BOIN-ET family

Source: vignettes/simFastBOIN-boin-et.Rmd
simFastBOIN-boin-et.Rmd

Why the optimal biological dose

For chemotherapy the most effective dose is usually taken to be the most toxic one that is still acceptable, the maximum tolerated dose (MTD). For targeted and immune therapies the response may level off, or even fall, below the MTD, and the aim is then the optimal biological dose (OBD), which weighs the response against the toxicity. The BOIN-ET design of Takeda, Taguri and Morita (2018) decides the next dose from both the DLT rate and the response rate at the current dose, and selects the OBD at the end of the trial.

The package provides three designs of this family:

  • BOIN-ET (Takeda et al., 2018), in which every cohort is assessed before the next one is dosed: sim_boin_et() and sim_boin_et_multi();
  • TITE-BOIN-ET (Takeda, Morita and Taguri, 2020), which doses new patients while earlier ones are still assessed: sim_tite_boin_et() and sim_tite_boin_et_multi();
  • BF-BOIN-ET (Takeda, Zhu and Hirakawa, 2025), which treats at lower doses the patients who arrive while a cohort is assessed: sim_bf_boin_et() and sim_bf_boin_et_multi().

The rules follow the R packages of the authors, ‘boinet’ (Yamaguchi, Takeda and Maruo, 2025) for the first two and ‘bfboinet’ for the third, with the changes described below. The trials and the selection of the OBD run in C++.

The boundaries and the decision table

The DLT rate at the current dose is compared with two boundaries, lambda1 and lambda2, and the response rate with one, eta1. They minimize the probability of an incorrect decision, as found by the grid search of boinet::gridoptim().

bd <- boin_et_boundary(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60)
bd
#> BOIN-ET boundaries
#>   target DLT rate      : 0.3
#>   target response rate : 0.6
#>   p_saf / p_tox        : 0.03 / 0.42
#>   p_saf_resp           : 0.36
#> 
#>   lambda1 (escalate)   : 0.14
#>   lambda2 (de-escalate): 0.35
#>   eta1 (response)      : 0.48
#>   probability of an incorrect decision: 0.04703

With a target DLT rate of 0.30, a target response rate of 0.60 and the design parameters of Takeda et al. (2018), the boundaries are 0.14 for lambda1, 0.35 for lambda2 and 0.48 for eta1, the values of the article. The decision at the current dose is then

  • E, escalate, when the DLT rate is at most lambda1 and the response rate at most eta1;
  • S, stay, when the DLT rate is below lambda2 and the response rate above eta1;
  • D, de-escalate, when the DLT rate is at least lambda2;
  • E/S/D otherwise, which moves to the dose with the highest observed response rate among the current dose and its neighbors, or escalates when the next higher dose has not been tried.
boin_et_decision_table(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60, n = c(3, 6))
#> BOIN-ET decision table
#>   lambda1 = 0.14, lambda2 = 0.35, eta1 = 0.48
#> 
#> 3 patients
#>     Responses
#> DLTs 0     1     2  3 
#>    0 E     E     S  S 
#>    1 E/S/D E/S/D S  S 
#>    2 D     D     D  D 
#>    3 D*    D*    D* D*
#> 
#> 6 patients
#>     Responses
#> DLTs 0     1     2     3  4  5  6 
#>    0 E     E     E     S  S  S  S 
#>    1 E/S/D E/S/D E/S/D S  S  S  S 
#>    2 E/S/D E/S/D E/S/D S  S  S  S 
#>    3 D     D     D     D  D  D  D 
#>    4 D*    D*    D*    D* D* D* D*
#>    5 D*    D*    D*    D* D* D* D*
#>    6 D*    D*    D*    D* D* D* D*
#> 
#> E = escalate, S = stay, D = de-escalate, E/S/D = choose among the current and neighboring doses;
#> * = the dose is no longer admissible

These are the decisions of Table 2 of Takeda et al. (2018). A star marks the counts that make a dose inadmissible: by default, as in ‘boinet’, a dose is excluded when the posterior probability that its DLT rate exceeds target is above cutoff_eli = 0.95, or when the posterior probability that its response rate is below p_saf_resp is above cutoff_eli_resp = 0.99. p_eli and p_eli_resp change the two rates; the simulations of the article exclude a dose when the posterior probability that its DLT rate is below 0.40 is less than 0.10, or that its response rate is above 0.20 is less than 0.10 (p_eli = 0.40, p_eli_resp = 0.20, cutoff_eli = 0.90 and cutoff_eli_resp = 0.90).

Operating characteristics for one scenario

Scenario 1 of Takeda et al. (2018) has six doses, twelve cohorts of three patients and a trial that starts at the lowest dose.

p_true <- c(0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40)
p_resp <- c(0.05, 0.35, 0.55, 0.65, 0.75, 0.70)

oc <- sim_boin_et(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60, p_true = p_true,
                  p_resp = p_resp, n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3,
                  n_trials = 2000, seed = 123)
oc
#> BOIN-ET operating characteristics
#>   target DLT rate      : 0.3
#>   target response rate : 0.6
#>   trials               : 2000
#>   cohorts              : 12 of size 3
#>   max sample size      : 36
#>   lambda1 / lambda2    : 0.14 / 0.35
#>   eta1                 : 0.48
#>   OBD selection        : max_resp with observed response rates
#> 
#>                        DL1  DL2  DL3  DL4  DL5  DL6 Total / No OBD
#> True DLT rate (%)      5.0 15.0 25.0 30.0 35.0 40.0               
#> True response rate (%) 5.0 35.0 55.0 65.0 75.0 70.0               
#> OBD selected (%)       1.5 16.1 47.1 26.7  7.0  0.5            1.1
#> Patients treated       3.5  8.9 14.3  7.1  1.8  0.2           35.8
#> Patients with DLT      0.2  1.3  3.6  2.2  0.6  0.1            8.0
#> Patients with response 0.2  3.1  7.9  4.7  1.4  0.1           17.3
#> 
#> Trials stopped early: 1.1%

The output gives the percentage of trials selecting each dose as the OBD, the average numbers of patients, DLTs and responses at each dose, and the percentage of trials stopped early. Here dose 3 is selected most often, in 47 percent of the trials, and 1.1 percent of the trials select no OBD.

Several scenarios are run with sim_boin_et_multi(). In scenario 7 of the article the response rate peaks at dose 2 while the DLT rate goes on rising.

scenarios <- list(
  list(name = "Scenario 1", p_true = p_true, p_resp = p_resp),
  list(name = "Scenario 7", p_true = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.45, 0.55),
       p_resp = c(0.30, 0.70, 0.60, 0.50, 0.40, 0.30))
)
sim_boin_et_multi(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60, scenarios = scenarios,
                  n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3, n_trials = 1000,
                  seed = 123)
#> BOIN-ET operating characteristics across 2 scenarios

Selecting the OBD

At the end of a trial the DLT rates of the doses tried are made monotone by isotonic regression, and the response rates are estimated with one of three estimators (est_method): the observed rates (the default), the model-averaged unimodal isotonic regression of Lin and Yin (2017) ("multi_iso"), or the fractional polynomial logistic regression of Takeda et al. (2018) ("fp_logistic", which needs the ‘mfp’ package). The OBD is then chosen among the admissible doses with one of four rules (obd_method): the highest estimated response rate up to the estimated MTD ("max_resp", the default), or the highest value of one of the three utilities compared by Yamaguchi et al. (2024) ("utility_weighted", "utility_truncated_linear" and "utility_scoring").

boin_et_select_obd() selects the OBD from the final data of trials, so the same simulated trials can be judged under every rule.

oc_kept <- sim_boin_et(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60, p_true = p_true,
                       p_resp = p_resp, n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3,
                       n_trials = 2000, keep_trials = TRUE, seed = 123)
tr <- oc_kept$trials

select_percent <- function(est_method, obd_method) {
  obd <- boin_et_select_obd(n_pts = tr$n_pts, n_tox = tr$n_tox,
                            n_resp = tr$n_resp, target = 0.30,
                            target_resp = 0.60, est_method = est_method,
                            obd_method = obd_method,
                            early_stop = tr$early_stop)$obd
  as.numeric(table(factor(obd, levels = 1:6))) / length(obd) * 100
}

rules <- c("max_resp", "utility_weighted", "utility_truncated_linear",
           "utility_scoring")
selection <- rbind(
  t(sapply(rules, function(m) select_percent("observed", m))),
  "max_resp, multi_iso" = select_percent("multi_iso", "max_resp")
)
colnames(selection) <- paste0("DL", 1:6)
round(selection, 1)
#>                          DL1  DL2  DL3  DL4  DL5 DL6
#> max_resp                 1.5 16.1 47.1 26.7  7.0 0.5
#> utility_weighted         1.5 16.4 44.0 28.5  7.6 0.8
#> utility_truncated_linear 5.9 34.3 39.1 15.7  3.3 0.4
#> utility_scoring          2.1 16.5 39.4 29.8 10.1 1.0
#> max_resp, multi_iso      0.2 14.4 48.9 27.7  7.0 0.5

all.equal(unname(selection["max_resp", ]), unname(oc_kept$sel_percent))
#> [1] TRUE

The first row is the selection of sim_boin_et(), which calls boin_et_select_obd() with the same defaults. The fractional polynomial is fitted once for every distinct set of final data and takes longer:

sim_boin_et(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60, p_true = p_true,
            p_resp = p_resp, n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3,
            n_trials = 2000, est_method = "fp_logistic", seed = 123)

Dose moves that differ from ‘boinet’

After each cohort the admissibility of every dose is derived again from its data, and the trial stops early when no dose is admissible, or when the dose should be lowered and no admissible dose is found at or below the intended one. When the intended dose is not admissible, a stay or a de-escalation moves to the highest admissible dose below it, and an escalation to the lowest admissible dose above it, or stays when there is none.

Two rules differ from those of ‘boinet’ 1.6.0. Takeda et al. (2018) do not allow dose skipping during escalation, so a dose excluded by its DLT data also excludes every higher dose, as in the later BF-BOIN-ET design and the ‘bfboinet’ package, and an escalation from the highest dose ends the trial when that dose is excluded. In ‘boinet’, an escalation can skip a dose excluded by its DLT data and reach an untried higher dose, and an escalation from the highest dose stays there even when it is excluded. boinet_compatible = TRUE applies these rules of ‘boinet’ in every BOIN-ET and TITE-BOIN-ET function.

skip_design <- list(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60,
                    p_true = c(0.10, 0.20, 0.45, 0.50, 0.55),
                    p_resp = c(0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50, 0.60),
                    n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3, n_trials = 2000,
                    seed = 123)
oc_default <- do.call(sim_boin_et, skip_design)
oc_boinet <- do.call(sim_boin_et,
                     c(skip_design, list(boinet_compatible = TRUE)))
round(rbind(default = oc_default$n_pts_dose,
            boinet = oc_boinet$n_pts_dose), 2)
#>          DL1   DL2  DL3  DL4  DL5
#> default 5.20 14.65 9.73 4.77 1.13
#> boinet  4.84 11.57 9.47 6.89 3.05

Doses 4 and 5, with DLT probabilities of 0.50 and 0.55, receive 5.9 patients per trial on average under the default rules and 9.9 under those of ‘boinet’, which let an escalation from dose 2 skip dose 3 once it is excluded.

TITE-BOIN-ET

When the DLT and the response take long to assess compared with the time between arrivals, TITE-BOIN-ET doses new patients while earlier ones are still assessed. A patient still under assessment counts in the DLT and response rates of a dose by the fraction of the window followed so far (Takeda et al., 2020), and the decision rule of BOIN-ET is applied to these rates. The admissibility of the doses counts such a patient as a patient without the event, as in ‘boinet’.

The first patient of a cohort arrives at the time of the previous decision, and the next decision is due when the next patient arrives. While fewer than a share min_completed_share of the patients at the current dose have finished both assessments, the decision waits for the next assessment to end. The default, 0.5, is the rule of boinet::tite.boinet(). The simulations of Takeda et al. (2020) did not wait (min_completed_share = 0), and the article recommends such a rule when the accrual is fast. By default the times to DLT and to response are Weibull, with late_fraction and resp_late_fraction of the events in the second half of each window, and they are linked by a Gaussian copula with correlation resp_cor.

The setting of Takeda et al. (2020) is a DLT window of 28 days, a response window of 56 days and one patient every 14 days; the unit of time is the day.

tite_design <- list(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60, p_true = p_true,
                    p_resp = p_resp, n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3,
                    window = 28, resp_window = 56, accrual_rate = 1 / 14,
                    n_trials = 1000, seed = 123)
oc_tite <- do.call(sim_tite_boin_et, tite_design)
oc_tite
#> TITE-BOIN-ET operating characteristics
#>   target DLT rate      : 0.3
#>   target response rate : 0.6
#>   trials               : 1000
#>   cohorts              : 12 of size 3
#>   max sample size      : 36
#>   lambda1 / lambda2    : 0.14 / 0.35
#>   eta1                 : 0.48
#>   OBD selection        : max_resp with observed response rates
#> 
#>                        DL1  DL2  DL3  DL4  DL5  DL6 Total / No OBD
#> True DLT rate (%)      5.0 15.0 25.0 30.0 35.0 40.0               
#> True response rate (%) 5.0 35.0 55.0 65.0 75.0 70.0               
#> OBD selected (%)       1.1 18.0 44.8 26.9  6.1  0.4            2.7
#> Patients treated       4.0  9.3 13.5  6.9  1.8  0.2           35.6
#> Patients with DLT      0.2  1.5  3.4  2.1  0.7  0.1            7.9
#> Patients with response 0.2  3.2  7.4  4.5  1.4  0.2           16.9
#> 
#> Trials stopped early: 2.7%
#> Average trial duration: 616.5

oc_tite_0 <- do.call(sim_tite_boin_et,
                     c(tite_design, list(min_completed_share = 0)))
round(rbind(
  "wait for half" = c(oc_tite$sel_percent, weeks = oc_tite$duration / 7),
  "no wait" = c(oc_tite_0$sel_percent, weeks = oc_tite_0$duration / 7)
), 1)
#>               DL1  DL2  DL3  DL4 DL5 DL6 weeks
#> wait for half 1.1 18.0 44.8 26.9 6.1 0.4  88.1
#> no wait       0.9 20.7 45.6 23.0 7.2 0.3  77.1

The trials last 88 weeks on average with the default rule and 77 weeks without waiting. The duration runs from the arrival of the first patient to the last decision, which is the end of both assessments of every patient when all cohorts are enrolled. The durations reported by Takeda et al. (2020) correspond to counting also the interval between arrivals before the first patient.

BF-BOIN-ET

In BF-BOIN-ET a cohort is treated at the current dose, and the next cohort starts with the first patient who arrives once the DLT outcomes of the cohort are known. The patients who arrive in between are backfilled one by one, when the current dose is not the lowest, to the lower dose with the highest utility among those with a promising response rate. The utility is defined by the scores psi00, psi01, psi10 and psi11 of a patient without DLT or response, with a DLT only, with a response only and with both. The dose escalation uses the DLT rate at the current dose with the boundaries of BOIN, and stays after 1 DLT in 3 patients. A dose with n_elimination patients or more is excluded for good when its DLT or response data are poor, a dose excluded by its DLT data taking every higher dose with it. The OBD is the admissible dose up to the estimated MTD with the highest utility. The rules are those of bfboinet::get.oc.backboinet().

The example of ‘bfboinet’ has five doses, ten cohorts of three, windows of one month and three patients a month; the unit of time is the month.

bf_design <- list(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.25,
                  p_true = c(0.03, 0.05, 0.20, 0.22, 0.45),
                  p_resp = c(0.05, 0.10, 0.50, 0.68, 0.70),
                  n_cohort = 10, cohort_size = 3, window = 1,
                  accrual_rate = 3, n_trials = 1000, seed = 123)
oc_bf <- do.call(sim_bf_boin_et, bf_design)
oc_bf
#> BF-BOIN-ET operating characteristics
#>   target DLT rate      : 0.3
#>   target response rate : 0.25
#>   trials               : 1000
#>   cohorts              : 10 of size 3
#>   patients per dose    : 12 at most with backfill
#>   lambda1 / lambda2    : 0.2365 / 0.3585
#>   eta1                 : 0.1968
#> 
#>                        DL1  DL2  DL3  DL4  DL5 Total / No OBD
#> True DLT rate (%)      3.0  5.0 20.0 22.0 45.0               
#> True response rate (%) 5.0 10.0 50.0 68.0 70.0               
#> OBD selected (%)       2.2  3.5 40.7 48.0  5.5            0.1
#> Patients treated       4.1  5.9 11.3  9.8  5.3           36.3
#> Patients backfilled    0.7  1.4  4.5  2.8  0.2            9.5
#> Patients with DLT      0.1  0.3  2.2  2.1  2.4            7.2
#> Patients with response 0.2  0.6  5.6  6.6  3.7           16.7
#> 
#> Trials stopped early: 0%
#> Average trial duration: 16.8

With suspend = 0.33 the next cohort may start while a third of the patients at the current dose are still assessed for DLT, which is the BF-BOIN-ET-A design of Takeda et al. (2025); the default, suspend = 0, is their BF-BOIN-ET-C design.

oc_bf_a <- do.call(sim_bf_boin_et, c(bf_design, list(suspend = 0.33)))
round(rbind(
  "BF-BOIN-ET-C" = c(oc_bf$sel_percent, patients = oc_bf$total_n_pts,
                     backfilled = oc_bf$total_n_bf,
                     months = oc_bf$duration),
  "BF-BOIN-ET-A" = c(oc_bf_a$sel_percent, patients = oc_bf_a$total_n_pts,
                     backfilled = oc_bf_a$total_n_bf,
                     months = oc_bf_a$duration)
), 1)
#>              DL1 DL2  DL3  DL4 DL5 patients backfilled months
#> BF-BOIN-ET-C 2.2 3.5 40.7 48.0 5.5     36.3        9.5   16.8
#> BF-BOIN-ET-A 3.2 3.5 40.7 45.6 6.2     33.6        6.1   13.3

The patients include the backfilled ones. The trials last 16.8 months on average under BF-BOIN-ET-C and 13.3 months under BF-BOIN-ET-A.

How the implementation is checked

The scripts in inst/reproduce/ and inst/validation/ compare the package with the articles and with the packages of the authors, and write the tables of judgments in their results/ folders, which are summarized here. A simulated cell passes when it lies within four standard errors of the difference between the two simulations plus the rounding of the published value.

  • Takeda et al. (2018). 68 of the 68 entries of the boundaries and of the decisions of Table 2 agree exactly. Of the 156 cells of Table 3, 142 pass; 10 of the 14 others are in scenario 11, where the printed response rate of 0.55 at the lowest dose does not fit the published results, and ‘boinet’ too selects that dose far more often than the article reports.
  • Takeda et al. (2020). Of the 324 cells of Table 2, 295 pass. The BOIN-ET rows fail in 12 cells, in scenario 11 and in the cells that also fail for Table 3 of the 2018 article. Of the 17 cells of TITE-BOIN-ET that fail, 8 are in scenario 11 and 6 are early terminations, durations and allocations in scenarios 8, 9, 10 and 12, which agree better with an exclusion of doses that uses only the patients whose outcomes are known; the article does not say which patients this rule uses, and the package keeps the rule of ‘boinet’. The remaining 3 are not explained. The durations are compared after adding the mean interval between arrivals before the first patient.
  • Takeda et al. (2025). 336 of the 336 cells of Tables 1 and 2 pass, with and without the suspension rule.
  • ‘boinet’. The operating characteristics of sim_boin_et() and sim_tite_boin_et() with boinet_compatible = TRUE are compared with those of boinet::boinet() and boinet::tite.boinet(): 312 of 312 cells pass for BOIN-ET and 196 of 196 for TITE-BOIN-ET. The packages draw their random numbers differently, so they agree in distribution, not trial by trial. The tests also compare the boundaries with boinet::gridoptim() and the OBD of simulated trials with boinet::obd.select() exactly.
  • ‘bfboinet’. 85 of the 85 cells comparing sim_bf_boin_et() with bfboinet::get.oc.backboinet() pass.
  • Separate implementations. The trials of the three engines agree exactly, trial by trial, with implementations written in Python from the R code of ‘boinet’ and ‘bfboinet’ and fed with the same random numbers.

References

Takeda, K., Taguri, M. and Morita, S. (2018). BOIN-ET: Bayesian optimal interval design for dose finding based on both efficacy and toxicity outcomes. Pharmaceutical Statistics, 17(4), 383-395.

Takeda, K., Morita, S. and Taguri, M. (2020). TITE-BOIN-ET: Time-to-event Bayesian optimal interval design to accelerate dose-finding based on both efficacy and toxicity outcomes. Pharmaceutical Statistics, 19(3), 335-349.

Takeda, K., Zhu, J. and Hirakawa, A. (2025). BF-BOIN-ET: A backfill Bayesian optimal interval design using efficacy and toxicity outcomes for dose optimization. Pharmaceutical Statistics, 24(2), e2470.

Yamaguchi, Y., Takeda, K. and Maruo, K. (2025). boinet: An R package for Bayesian optimal interval design for dose finding based on both efficacy and toxicity outcomes. The R Journal, 17(2), 15-34.

Yamaguchi, Y., Takeda, K., Yoshida, S. and Maruo, K. (2024). Optimal biological dose selection in dose-finding trials with model-assisted designs based on efficacy and toxicity: a simulation study. Journal of Biopharmaceutical Statistics, 34(3), 379-393.

Lin, R. and Yin, G. (2017). STEIN: A simple toxicity and efficacy interval design for seamless phase I/II clinical trials. Statistics in Medicine, 36(26), 4106-4120.
